transcript.text: people say AI can predict no-shows. is that real or hype?

It's real, with limits. If you have a record of past appointments, a model can often tell which ones are riskier than others. Lead time, a client's history of missed visits, the day and time, and whether a reminder went out are common signals. It can't say with certainty who will skip. It gives each booking a likelihood. Whether that's worth having depends on what you'd do with it, such as sending extra reminders, overbooking slightly, or calling people to confirm. If you can't act on the prediction, it's mostly hype. What's your situation? What kind of appointments or bookings do you have, and what would you change if you knew in advance which ones were likely to be missed?

What kind of appointments or bookings do you have, and what would you change if you knew in advance which ones were likely to be no-shows?

Mostly regular dental stuff. Cleanings, checkups, some fillings. We have 3 dentists. If we knew which ones were likely to skip, I guess we'd call those people to confirm, or try to fill the slot from our waitlist. I'm not sure how much that would save us, though. We have records in our booking software, I think going back about 2 years.

That helps. You'd call the risky bookings to confirm, or offer the slot to your waitlist, and you want to know if it's worth it. The records are the next thing I need. Can you export them from your booking software, and do they show which appointments were missed? If you can share them, I can first work out how many appointments you lose to no-shows now. That number tells us what a prediction could save before we build anything.

Not sure if it marks missed ones. I haven't exported anything yet. Honestly I'm really just trying to figure out if this is worth paying someone for, or if I should just send more reminder texts. Is there a quick way to check the missed ones before I hand over any data?

Yes, you can check this yourself before sharing anything. 1. **Find the missed ones.** Look in your booking software for an appointment status or report called something like "no-show", "missed", "failed" or "broken appointments". Filter it to the last 3 months and note how many appointments were booked in total. Late cancellations often get their own status, so keep them separate. They hurt too, but the fix is different. 2. **Turn the count into money.** Take the missed appointments per week and multiply by what an average slot is worth to you. That's roughly what's at stake each year. It's also the most a prediction could ever save you. It would only recover part of that, because some of those people can't be reached and some slots can't be refilled. 3. **Read the result.**
   - If you lose only a few slots a week, more reminders and a waitlist are probably enough, and paying someone for a model likely isn't worth it. - If you lose a lot, and reminders are already going out, a model that picks out the risky bookings for a call starts to make sense. If your software has no status for missed visits, that's worth knowing now. A model learns from past misses, so without a marker there is nothing to learn from. In that case the cheaper first step is to start recording them. Do you already send reminder texts today? If you do, how far ahead do they go out?

I've logged this as a plain-advice answer, and it needs none of your data. Next, check your software for a missed-appointment status or report. Count the missed ones over the last 3 months against everything booked. If you find it, bring me the counts, or share an export later, and I can help you work out what a prediction could realistically save.
Yeah, we send texts already. I'm not sure how far ahead though, the front desk sets that up. I'll look for the missed ones in the software. Still not sure it's worth paying someone for, honestly.

Your doubt is reasonable, and I wouldn't pay anyone yet. The count of missed visits decides it. If you lose only a few slots a week, better-timed reminders and your waitlist will probably do the job. The reminder timing is also worth a quick question to the front desk. When the texts go out can matter as much as how many you send. One thing would help me shape any advice: if a booking were flagged as risky, who would make the confirmation call and try to fill the slot from the waitlist? Is that you, or the front desk?

If a booking were flagged as likely to be missed, who would make the confirmation call and try to fill the slot from the waitlist? Is that you, or the front desk?
Probably the front desk. They handle the bookings and the texts. I'm not really sure, though. I'd have to ask them. Honestly I'm not even sure we'd have time to call people.

That's useful to know, and it matters. A model only pays off if someone has time to act on what it flags. If the front desk is already stretched, a list of risky bookings to call won't help much. You'd get more from things that need no calls, like texts people reply to in order to confirm, or a simple rule for offering freed-up slots to your waitlist.

Picture a short list each morning of the handful of bookings most likely to be missed that week. Could your front desk make a few calls from it, or is even that more than they can fit in?
Not sure, honestly. I'd have to ask the front desk. Maybe a few calls a day, but I don't know. I also haven't looked at the software for the missed ones yet.

That's fine, and I wouldn't pay anyone yet. Two checks would settle most of this, and both are quick. In the software, count the missed visits over the last 3 months. Then ask the front desk when the reminder texts go out and whether a few calls a day are realistic. From there I can do one of two things. I can write a short brief now that sets out the break-even with rough figures: how many missed slots a week it takes before paying for prediction beats better reminders. Or I can wait for your real counts, or an export, and work from those. Which would be more useful to you?
Maybe the quick version now, so I know what numbers I'm aiming for. I'll look at the software and ask the front desk about the texts and calls, then come back with what they say.

- **The break-even.** It sets out how many missed slots a week it takes before paying for prediction beats better reminders and your waitlist. transcript.text: quick q: churn with 3% positives, should i report PR-AUC or ROC-AUC to my manager, and why? no data work, just the answer

Report PR-AUC as your headline number. If your manager expects to see ROC-AUC, put it next to PR-AUC as a secondary figure. ROC-AUC can look good when the model isn't. It is built on the false positive rate, and that rate is measured against the large majority of customers who don't churn. A model can flag many non-churners and still have a small false positive rate. ROC-AUC can then look strong even though most of the people you'd contact are not going to leave. PR-AUC measures what your retention team deals with. It tracks precision (of the people we flag, how many really churn) against recall (of the people who churn, how many we catch). It ignores the large pool of easy true negatives. When you present it:
- **Give the baseline.** A model with no skill has a PR-AUC equal to the churn rate, which for you is the 3% you mentioned. Show your model's PR-AUC next to that figure so your manager can see how much better than chance it is. - **Add one business-level figure.** For example: "if we contact the top slice of customers by risk, this share of them churn, and we reach this share of all churners." A manager can act on that more easily than on any AUC. - **Don't compare PR-AUC across datasets with different churn rates.** It depends on the base rate. ROC-AUC does not. - **Compute both on held-out data.** Use data the model never trained on. That's the full answer, and I haven't done any work on your data. If you later want to measure a real model this way, share the table and we can do it then.

1. Count and mean tenure by signup year and churn:
```sql
SELECT EXTRACT(YEAR FROM signup_date) AS signup_year,
       churned_next_month,
       COUNT(*) AS n,
       AVG(tenure_months) AS mean_tenure,
       MIN(tenure_months) AS min_tenure,
       MAX(tenure_months) AS max_tenure
FROM customers
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2;
```

2. The direct snapshot test, which is the implied reference date (signup_date + tenure_months) by churn group:
```sql
SELECT churned_next_month,
       COUNT(*) AS n,
       MIN(d) AS earliest,
       MAX(d) AS latest,
       COUNT(DISTINCT DATE_TRUNC('month', d)) AS distinct_months
FROM (SELECT churned_next_month,
             signup_date + tenure_months * INTERVAL '1 month' AS d
      FROM customers) t
GROUP BY 1;
```
